questions.command_term: Calculate, Show that, State, Determine, Describe
questions.question:
Monochromatic light of wavelength $\lambda=589\ \mathrm{nm}$ falls normally on a double slit. The centres of the two slits are separated by $d=0.400\ \mathrm{mm}$ and each slit has width $b=0.100\ \mathrm{mm}$. The interference pattern is observed on a screen at a distance $D=2.00\ \mathrm{m}$ from the slits. The angles involved are small enough that $\sin\theta\approx\tan\theta\approx\theta$ in radians, where convenient.

(a)

Calculate the separation of adjacent bright fringes in the interference pattern.

[3]

(b)

Calculate the distance from the centre of the pattern to the first minimum of the single-slit diffraction envelope.

[3]

(c)

Show that the fourth-order bright fringe is missing from the pattern, and state which other orders would be missing if the screen were large enough to show them.

[5]

(d)

Determine the number of bright fringes that are visible within the central maximum of the envelope.

[3]

(e)

The source is replaced by a white light source. Describe one change to the pattern, and explain it.

[2]
questions.answer:
(a) $s=\dfrac{\lambda D}{d}=\dfrac{589\times 10^{-9}\times 2.00}{0.400\times 10^{-3}}$ (M1) $=2.94\times 10^{-3}\ \mathrm{m}=2.94\ \mathrm{mm}$. (A1)

So adjacent bright fringes are $2.94\ \mathrm{mm}$ apart. (A1)

(b) The first minimum of the single-slit envelope is at the smallest angle satisfying $b\sin\theta=\lambda$: (M1)

$\sin\theta=\dfrac{\lambda}{b}=\dfrac{589\times 10^{-9}}{0.100\times 10^{-3}}=5.89\times 10^{-3}$ (A1)

The distance from the centre is $y=D\tan\theta\approx 2.00\times 5.89\times 10^{-3}=1.18\times 10^{-2}\ \mathrm{m}=11.8\ \mathrm{mm}$. (A1)

(c) A double-slit maximum of order $n$ occurs where $d\sin\theta=n\lambda$; the first single-slit minimum occurs where $b\sin\theta=\lambda$. (M1)

These coincide when $\dfrac{n\lambda}{d}=\dfrac{\lambda}{b}$, that is when $n=\dfrac{d}{b}$. (M1)

Here $\dfrac{d}{b}=\dfrac{0.400}{0.100}=4.0$ (A1), so the third-order condition places the minimum at $\theta$ with $\sin\theta=\dfrac{4\lambda}{d}=\dfrac{4\times 589\times 10^{-9}}{0.400\times 10^{-3}}=5.89\times 10^{-3}$, exactly the angle found in part (b). The fourth-order maximum therefore falls on a minimum of the envelope and is not visible. (A1)

More generally the missing orders are multiples of $d/b$, so orders $4,\ 8,\ 12,\ \ldots$ are missing. (A1) Order 8 would require $\sin\theta=\dfrac{8\lambda}{d}=1.18\times 10^{-2}$, which is still less than $1$, so order 8 is geometrically accessible and would also be missing. Orders beyond the first few visible ones fall outside the envelope's central region anyway.

(d) Within the central maximum of the envelope, $\left|\sin\theta\right|<\dfrac{\lambda}{b}$, so the allowed orders satisfy $\left|n\right|<\dfrac{d}{b}=4$. (M1)

So $n=-3,\,-2,\,-1,\,0,\,1,\,2,\,3$ are present (A1), giving seven bright fringes. (A1) Orders $n=\pm 4$ coincide exactly with the envelope minima from part (c) and are not visible.

(e) Each order becomes a continuous spectrum with the same angular spread, with red deviated most because $\theta$ increases with $\lambda$; the central maximum remains white since all wavelengths coincide there and it has no order number. (A1)(A1) Higher-order spectra overlap, so beyond the first order the colours are no longer separated cleanly.
questions.explanation:
This question is about two patterns with different length scales occupying the same screen, and about the fact that one of them governs the other. The double-slit fringes are set by $d$; the envelope is set by $b$; and because the two slits have a finite width, the brightness of the fringes is modulated by the diffraction of each individual slit. The envelope is not a curiosity — it determines which fringes exist.

The key step in part (c) is setting the two conditions equal. Because the fringe order is an integer and the ratio $d/b$ is exactly 4, the fourth-order maximum lands precisely on the first envelope minimum. The general result is worth remembering in the form 'orders that are multiples of $d/b$ are missing', and the follow-up question — whether those orders are actually reachable — is what distinguishes a complete answer. With $d/b=4$, order 8 requires $\sin\theta\approx 0.0118$, which is small, so it is reachable and also missing; a student who stops at 'four and eight are missing' without checking is right by luck rather than by reasoning, and the markscheme is written to notice the difference.

Part (d) converts a counting problem into an inequality. The central maximum of the envelope spans $\left|\sin\theta\right|<\lambda/b$, and within it the double-slit maxima satisfy $\left|n\right|<d/b=4$. The integers strictly between $-4$ and $4$ are seven, not nine, because the boundary values are exactly the missing orders. Students who count the boundaries produce nine and have not connected the two parts.

The final part moves from monochromatic light to white light, where each order becomes a spectrum. The central maximum stays white because the path difference is zero for every wavelength simultaneously; every other order is dispersed, with red deviated most. This is the observation that makes a diffraction grating a spectrometer rather than a decoration, and it is worth being able to state in one sentence.

questions.subject: Physics HL
questions.topic: Theme A: Space, time and motion
questions.question:
The belt moves at a constant speed $v=2.0\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$ and the gravel is delivered at a constant rate of $12\ \mathrm{kg\,s^{-1}}$.

(a)

Show that the horizontal force the belt must exert on the gravel is $F=v\dfrac{\Delta m}{\Delta t}$, and calculate the value of $F$.

[4]

(b)

Calculate the rate at which kinetic energy is supplied to the gravel as it is brought up to the belt's speed.

[4]

(c)

Show that the power delivered by the belt's motor is twice the rate at which the gravel gains kinetic energy, identify where the remaining energy goes, and hence calculate the efficiency with which the motor's work becomes kinetic energy of the gravel.

[5]

(d)

The belt speed is increased to $4.0\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$ while the mass flow rate is unchanged. Determine the new motor power and explain why it is not simply double the original power.

[3]
questions.answer:
(a) In a time interval $\Delta t$ a mass $\Delta m=\dfrac{\Delta m}{\Delta t}\Delta t$ of gravel is brought from rest to the belt's speed $v$. Its horizontal momentum therefore changes by $\Delta m\,v$, so the required horizontal force is

$$F=\frac{\Delta(mv)}{\Delta t}=v\frac{\Delta m}{\Delta t}$$ (M1)(AG)

Numerically,

$$F=2.0\times 12=24\ \mathrm{N}$$ (A1)(A1)

(b) Each second a mass of $12\ \mathrm{kg}$ is accelerated from rest to $2.0\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$, so the rate at which kinetic energy is supplied is

$$\frac{\Delta E_{k}}{\Delta t}=\tfrac12\frac{\Delta m}{\Delta t}v^{2}=\tfrac12(12)(2.0)^{2}$$ (M1)(A1)

$$=24\ \mathrm{W}$$ (A1)(A1)

(c) The belt moves at constant speed, so the motor's power equals the force it exerts multiplied by the belt's speed:

$$P=Fv=(24)(2.0)=48\ \mathrm{W}$$ (M1)(A1)

The ratio is

$$\frac{P}{\Delta E_{k}/\Delta t}=\frac{48}{24}=2$$ (A1)

so the motor supplies twice the rate at which the gravel gains kinetic energy. The remaining $24\ \mathrm{W}$ is dissipated as heat where the gravel slides against the belt while it is being accelerated: the friction force acts over the belt's displacement, which is larger than the gravel's displacement, and the difference appears as thermal energy at the sliding contact. (A1) The efficiency is therefore

$$\eta=\frac{24}{48}=0.50=50\%.$$ (A1)

(d) Since $F=v\dfrac{\Delta m}{\Delta t}$, doubling $v$ doubles the force to $48\ \mathrm{N}$. The power is $P=Fv$, and both the force and the belt speed have doubled, so

$$P=48\times 4.0=192\ \mathrm{W},$$ (M1)(A1)

which is four times the original $48\ \mathrm{W}$. Equivalently $P=\dfrac{\Delta m}{\Delta t}v^{2}\propto v^{2}$, because the belt must accelerate twice as much momentum each second and must do so through twice the distance per second. The mass flow rate has not changed, so the factor of four comes entirely from the doubling of both quantities in $P=Fv$, not from any change in the amount of gravel handled. (A1)

The efficiency is unchanged at $50\%$ when the speed doubles, and it is in fact fixed at $50\%$ for any belt speed and any mass flow rate, because the kinetic-energy rate and the motor power are both proportional to $\dfrac{\Delta m}{\Delta t}v^{2}$ and their ratio is therefore constant. It would rise above $50\%$ only if the gravel arrived already moving with the belt, so that less sliding were needed to bring it up to speed; the loss is a property of picking the mass up from rest, not of how fast the belt runs.
questions.explanation:
This question is built on a result that contradicts the energy audit most students perform automatically. The gravel gains kinetic energy at $24\ \mathrm{W}$, so it is natural to conclude that the motor must supply $24\ \mathrm{W}$. It does not: the motor supplies $48\ \mathrm{W}$, and the other $24\ \mathrm{W}$ is dissipated as heat where the gravel slides against the belt.

The reason is that work is force multiplied by the displacement of the point of application. The belt's friction force acts on the gravel, but the belt itself moves further than the gravel does while the gravel is catching up. In one second the belt advances $2.0\ \mathrm{m}$, whereas the gravel being accelerated moves on average only $1.0\ \mathrm{m}$, so the motor does $24\ \mathrm{N}\times 2.0\ \mathrm{m}=48\ \mathrm{J}$ of work while the gravel's kinetic energy rises by only $24\ \mathrm{J}$. The difference is the frictional heating at the sliding interface.

This is the same mechanism that heats a car's clutch during a standing start, and it is why the efficiency of any device that picks up a fresh charge of mass from rest by dragging it along at a fixed speed is capped at 50%. It is not a machine fault; it is a consequence of the inelastic way the mass is acquired.

Part (d) turns the result into a scaling law. The force is $F=\dfrac{\Delta m}{\Delta t}v$, proportional to $v$, and the power is $Fv$, so $P=\dfrac{\Delta m}{\Delta t}v^{2}$. Doubling the belt speed therefore doubles the force and doubles the speed through which that force acts, giving four times the power — a trap for candidates who expect a linear response.

Classic wrong turns: using $\tfrac12 mv^{2}$ to find the force; forgetting that it is the belt's displacement, not the gravel's, that sets the work done by the motor; and assuming that a constant-speed belt does no net work because the gravel's kinetic energy ends up steady. That last error confuses a steady state with a closed system.

questions.subject: Physics HL
questions.subtopic: C.1 Simple harmonic motion and C.2 Wave model
questions.question:
Two identical gliders, each of mass $m=0.020\ \mathrm{kg}$, rest on a frictionless horizontal air track. Each glider is held to a fixed post by a spring of stiffness $k=2.0\times10^{4}\ \mathrm{N\,m^{-1}}$, and the two gliders are joined to each other by a coupling spring of stiffness $k_{c}=3.0\times10^{4}\ \mathrm{N\,m^{-1}}$ (see the figure). The left glider carries a light piston that closes the near end of a long straight tube; the far end of the tube is lined with an absorber, so a travelling wave rather than a standing wave is set up, and when the glider moves along the track the piston drives a longitudinal compression wave along the tube. The speed of sound in the air in the tube is $340\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$. Friction, the mass of the springs and the mass of the piston are all negligible.

(a)

The two gliders are displaced by equal amounts in the same direction and released from rest. Show that the coupling spring is neither stretched nor compressed at any instant, deduce that the period of this motion is $T_{s}=2\pi\sqrt{m/k}$, and calculate the value of $T_{s}$.

[4]

(b)

The gliders are now displaced by equal amounts in opposite directions and released from rest. Determine the period $T_{a}$ of this motion, showing how the coupling spring now contributes, and calculate the ratio $T_{s}/T_{a}$.

[4]

(c)

In the antisymmetric motion the piston drives the wave in the tube at the frequency $f=1/T_{a}$. Calculate the frequency, the wavelength of the wave in the tube, and the phase difference between two points on the tube axis that are $0.534\ \mathrm{m}$ apart. State which of the two points is ahead in phase.

[4]

(d)

Show that $T_{s}/T_{a}=\sqrt{1+2k_{c}/k}$, and hence determine the value of this ratio in the limits $k_{c}\to0$ and $k_{c}\to\infty$. Explain what each limit means physically for the motion of the two gliders.

[4]
questions.answer:
(a) In this motion the two gliders have equal displacements in the same direction at every instant, so $x_{1}=x_{2}$ and their separation never changes; the coupling spring therefore remains at its natural length and exerts no force on either glider. (M1) Each glider is then acted on only by its own wall spring, so Newton's second law for either glider gives

$$m\ddot{x}=-kx\quad\Rightarrow\quad\ddot{x}=-\frac{k}{m}x.$$ (A1)

Comparing with the defining equation of simple harmonic motion, $a=-\omega^{2}x$, shows that $\omega_{s}=\sqrt{k/m}$ and hence

$$T_{s}=2\pi\sqrt{\frac{m}{k}}=2\pi\sqrt{\frac{0.020}{2.0\times10^{4}}}=2\pi\sqrt{1.0\times10^{-6}}$$ (A1)

$$T_{s}=6.28\times10^{-3}\ \mathrm{s}=6.28\ \mathrm{ms}.$$ (A1)

The coupling stiffness $k_{c}$ does not appear: in this mode the coupling spring is inert.

(b) In the antisymmetric motion $x_{1}=-x_{2}$, so the separation of the gliders changes by $2x_{1}$ and the coupling spring is stretched or compressed by twice the displacement of either glider. (M1) Its force on a glider is therefore $-k_{c}(2x_{1})$, and combining this with the wall spring gives

$$m\ddot{x}_{1}=-kx_{1}-2k_{c}x_{1}=-(k+2k_{c})x_{1},$$ (A1)

so $\omega_{a}=\sqrt{(k+2k_{c})/m}$ and

$$T_{a}=2\pi\sqrt{\frac{m}{k+2k_{c}}}=2\pi\sqrt{\frac{0.020}{2.0\times10^{4}+2(3.0\times10^{4})}}=2\pi\sqrt{\frac{0.020}{8.0\times10^{4}}}=2\pi\sqrt{2.5\times10^{-7}}$$

$$T_{a}=3.14\times10^{-3}\ \mathrm{s}=3.14\ \mathrm{ms}.$$ (A1)

The ratio of the two periods is

$$\frac{T_{s}}{T_{a}}=\sqrt{\frac{k+2k_{c}}{k}}=\sqrt{\frac{8.0\times10^{4}}{2.0\times10^{4}}}=2.00.$$ (A1)

The antisymmetric mode is therefore the faster of the two.

(c) The piston is driven by the glider that moves in the antisymmetric mode, so the frequency of the wave in the tube is fixed by $T_{a}$:

$$f=\frac{1}{T_{a}}=\frac{1}{3.1416\times10^{-3}}=318\ \mathrm{Hz}.$$ (M1)(A1)

Using the wave equation $v=f\lambda$,

$$\lambda=\frac{v}{f}=\frac{340}{318.3}=1.07\ \mathrm{m}.$$ (A1)

The phase difference between two points separated by $\Delta x=0.534\ \mathrm{m}$ is

$$\Delta\varphi=\frac{2\pi\,\Delta x}{\lambda}=\frac{2\pi(0.534)}{1.068}=3.14\ \mathrm{rad}=\pi.$$ (A1)

The two points are in antiphase. The point nearer the piston is ahead in phase: the disturbance reaches it first, and the farther point lags by the propagation delay $\Delta x/v=1.57\ \mathrm{ms}$, which is exactly half a period.

(d) Dividing the two periods,

$$\frac{T_{s}}{T_{a}}=\sqrt{\frac{k+2k_{c}}{k}}=\sqrt{1+\frac{2k_{c}}{k}}.$$ (M1)

As $k_{c}\to0$ the ratio tends to $1$, so $T_{a}\to T_{s}$. The coupling spring has gone, the two gliders are independent identical oscillators, and every possible motion is a superposition of one single frequency; the distinction between the symmetric and the antisymmetric mode therefore disappears. (A1)

As $k_{c}\to\infty$ the ratio diverges and $T_{a}\to0$. An infinitely stiff coupling spring holds the gliders a fixed distance apart, so they can no longer move in opposite directions and the antisymmetric mode is suppressed. (A1)

For any finite $k_{c}$ the ratio is greater than one, so the antisymmetric mode is always the faster of the two, while the symmetric period is completely independent of $k_{c}$. (A1)
questions.explanation:
The question is built on a single point of physics: in the symmetric normal mode of this system the coupling spring does not change length, so it cannot affect the period. A candidate who has met a coupled oscillator reaches for the coupling stiffness, and the natural guess is that the period must involve $k+k_{c}$ or $k+2k_{c}$. In the symmetric mode it involves neither; only the wall springs and the mass appear, and the period is exactly that of a single glider on its own wall spring.

The reason is that the two gliders move as one. Their separation is constant, the coupling spring stays at its natural length, and it pulls on neither glider. The wall springs are the only sources of restoring force, and each acts on its own glider, so the two oscillators are independent and identical. The coupling spring matters only in the antisymmetric mode, where the gliders move towards and away from each other: the separation changes by twice the displacement of one glider, so the spring's extension is doubled and its effective stiffness is $2k_{c}$. This is the familiar result that a spring pulled from both ends behaves as though it were twice as stiff.

Part (c) forces the SHM result to do work. The wave frequency is not chosen by the candidate; it is fixed by $T_{a}$, and the wavelength then follows from $v=f\lambda$. The phase difference is the wave-model consequence: two points half a wavelength apart are in antiphase, and the point nearer the source leads. A candidate who uses the naive $f=\sqrt{k/m}/(2\pi)$, the symmetric frequency, will obtain a wavelength twice too large and a phase difference half the correct value; the question separates those two frequencies deliberately.

Part (d) turns the result into a limit. Writing the ratio as $\sqrt{1+2k_{c}/k}$ makes both limits visible. As the coupling stiffness vanishes the two frequencies coalesce, which is the signature of a degeneracy: without coupling there is no way to tell the 'symmetric' mode from the 'antisymmetric' one, because the two gliders are simply independent. As the coupling stiffness becomes very large the gliders are locked a fixed distance apart and the antisymmetric motion is frozen out.

Classic wrong turns: assuming that the coupling spring contributes to the symmetric mode; treating the two gliders as a single mass $2m$ on a single spring, which happens to give the right answer here only because of the factor of two; and using the symmetric frequency rather than the antisymmetric one to drive the wave.

questions.subject: Physics HL
questions.question:
A string of length $L=0.80\ \mathrm{m}$ is stretched between two rigid supports with a tension $T=24\ \mathrm{N}$. Its linear mass density is $\mu=0.015\ \mathrm{kg\,m^{-1}}$, and the tension may be taken as uniform along the whole string. A player lightly touches the string at a point a distance $d$ from the left support, holding that point fixed, and then sets the string vibrating; the touch forces a node at that point but does not otherwise alter the string. Only a standing wave that already has a node at the touched point can be excited.

(a)

Calculate the speed of transverse waves on the string, and calculate the frequencies of the first three standing-wave modes of the string when it is not touched.

[4]

(b)

With the string touched at $d=0.30\ \mathrm{m}$, show that a standing wave can be excited only if the mode number $n$ satisfies $d=jL/n$ for some integer $j$, deduce that $n$ must be a multiple of $8$, and hence determine the lowest frequency that the touched string can produce.

[5]

(c)

Determine the frequencies of the next two modes that the touched string can produce, and determine the total number of nodes, including the two fixed ends, in the lowest of these allowed modes. State how many of the untouched harmonics below that lowest allowed frequency are absent.

[4]

(d)

The player now touches the string at its midpoint instead. Explain how the set of allowed modes changes, determine the new lowest frequency, and explain why every odd harmonic is now missing.

[3]
questions.answer:
(a) For a stretched string the wave speed is given by $v=\sqrt{T/\mu}$: (M1)

$$v=\sqrt{\frac{24}{0.015}}=\sqrt{1600}=40\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}.$$ (A1)

The standing-wave condition for a string fixed at both ends is $L=n\lambda/2$, so $f_{n}=nv/(2L)$: (M1)

$$f_{n}=\frac{n(40)}{2(0.80)}=25n\ \mathrm{Hz},$$

giving $f_{1}=25\ \mathrm{Hz}$, $f_{2}=50\ \mathrm{Hz}$ and $f_{3}=75\ \mathrm{Hz}$. (A1)

(b) A standing wave on the string has zero displacement at every node, and the nodes of the $n$th mode lie at distances $x_{j}=jL/n$ from the left support, with $j=0,1,2,\dots,n$. (M1) The touched point is held fixed, so it must be a node, and therefore $d=jL/n$ for some integer $j$. (A1) Substituting $d=0.30\ \mathrm{m}$ and $L=0.80\ \mathrm{m}$,

$$n=\frac{jL}{d}=\frac{j(0.80)}{0.30}=\frac{8j}{3}.$$ (A1)

For $n$ to be an integer, $j$ must be a multiple of $3$, so $j=3,6,9,\dots$ and the mode number must be $n=8,16,24,\dots$ — a multiple of $8$. (A1) The lowest allowed mode is therefore $n=8$, with frequency

$$f=\frac{8v}{2L}=\frac{8(40)}{1.60}=200\ \mathrm{Hz}.$$ (A1)

(c) The next two allowed modes are $n=16$ and $n=24$: (M1)

$$f_{16}=16\times25=400\ \mathrm{Hz},\qquad f_{24}=24\times25=600\ \mathrm{Hz}.$$ (A1)

In the $n=8$ mode the nodes lie at $x_{j}=j(0.80)/8=0.10j\ \mathrm{m}$ for $j=0,1,\dots,8$, that is at $0.00,0.10,0.20,\dots,0.80\ \mathrm{m}$. Counting the two fixed ends, there are $9$ nodes in all. (A1) The untouched harmonics below $200\ \mathrm{Hz}$ are $25,50,75,100,125,150$ and $175\ \mathrm{Hz}$ — seven of them — and all seven are absent. (A1)

(d) Touching at the midpoint sets $d=L/2$, so $n=jL/d=2j$ and only even mode numbers survive: the allowed frequencies are $50,100,150,\dots\ \mathrm{Hz}$. (M1) The new lowest frequency is therefore the second harmonic,

$$f=\frac{2v}{2L}=\frac{2(40)}{1.60}=50\ \mathrm{Hz}.$$ (A1)

Every odd harmonic has an antinode at the midpoint, so holding the midpoint fixed suppresses all of them; only the even harmonics, which already have a node there, are unaffected. (A1) In general a touch at a distance $L/p$ from one end selects the harmonics whose numbers are multiples of $p$: the midpoint touch ($p=2$) keeps the even harmonics, and the one-third touch ($p=3$) keeps every third.
questions.explanation:
A stretched string fixed at both ends is the standard example of a harmonic series, and the result $f_{n}=nv/(2L)$ is the first thing a candidate reaches for. The question is designed so that this formula is not the answer. Touching the string at a point does not divide it into two independent strings; it forces a node there, and the whole string must still vibrate as a single standing wave. The modes that can be excited are therefore exactly those whose own node pattern already contains the touched point.

For a mode with $n$ half-wavelengths along the string, the nodes lie at $jL/n$. Requiring one of them to coincide with the touch at $d$ gives $d=jL/n$, or $n=jL/d$. With $d=0.30\ \mathrm{m}$ and $L=0.80\ \mathrm{m}$ this is $n=8j/3$, and because $n$ must be an integer the smallest possible mode number is $8$, not $1$ and not $3$. The lowest note the touched string can give is the eighth harmonic, at $200\ \mathrm{Hz}$ — eight times the fundamental.

The arithmetic is a number-theoretic condition rather than an algebraic one: the touch point is three-eighths of the way along, and $8/3$ only becomes an integer when it is multiplied by three. This is why the familiar cases are the easy ones. Touching at the midpoint gives $n=2j$ and the even harmonics; touching at one third of the length gives $n=3j$ and the third, sixth and ninth. The three-eighths position is deliberately not one of these, so a candidate who tries to generalise from the familiar cases without deriving the node condition will fail.

Part (c) also asks for the node count, which tests whether the candidate has understood that the touched point is a node and not a new end: the eighth mode has nine nodes, not eight, because the two fixed ends count.

The classic wrong turns are: quoting $f_{n}=nv/(2L)$ and reporting $25\ \mathrm{Hz}$ as the lowest available note; treating the touch as cutting the string into two separate strings of length $0.30\ \mathrm{m}$ and $0.50\ \mathrm{m}$ and searching for their common resonances, which can give the right number for the wrong reason; and forgetting that the fixed ends are nodes when counting. There is also a practical check worth making: on a real instrument the touched harmonic is much weaker than the open string, because the finger damps the other modes and forces the energy into the one pattern that has a node beneath it.

questions.subject: Physics HL
questions.topic: Theme E: Nuclear and quantum physics
questions.subtopic: E.1 Structure of the atom / E.2 Quantum physics
questions.question:
Assume that the light from each line is monochromatic and that the photocell is ideal, so that the stopping voltage corresponds to the maximum kinetic energy of the emitted electrons. The values of the Planck constant and the speed of light are not needed.

(a)

Explain why the stopping voltage measures the maximum kinetic energy of the photoelectrons, and state the photoelectric equation that relates the stopping voltage, the photon energy and the work function of the cathode.

[3]

(b)

Show that the photon energies of the $n=4\to2$ and $n=2\to1$ transitions of this ion are $\dfrac{3A}{16}$ and $\dfrac{3A}{4}$ respectively, and state which of the two measured stopping voltages corresponds to each transition.

[4]

(c)

Using the two measured stopping voltages, determine the value of $A$ and the work function $\phi$ of the cathode, and explain why neither stopping voltage on its own is sufficient to find $\phi$.

[5]

(d)

Determine the nuclear charge number $Z$ of the ion and its ionisation energy in electronvolts, and explain how the wavelengths of the two spectral lines would change if the gas were replaced by a hydrogen-like ion of larger $Z$.

[4]
questions.answer:
(a) The emitted photoelectrons have a range of kinetic energies up to a maximum $K_{\max}$. (A1) The stopping voltage is the reverse potential difference that just reduces the photocurrent to zero, so it removes the kinetic energy of the fastest electrons: $eV_{s}=K_{\max}$. (A1) Energy conservation for the absorption of a single photon gives $hf=\phi+K_{\max}$, and therefore

$$eV_{s}=hf-\phi$$ (A1)

(b) The energy of the photon emitted in a transition equals the difference between the two levels involved. (M1) For $n=4\to2$,

$$hf_{1}=E_{4}-E_{2}=-\frac{A}{16}-\left(-\frac{A}{4}\right)=\frac{A}{4}-\frac{A}{16}=\frac{3A}{16}$$ (A1)

and for $n=2\to1$,

$$hf_{2}=E_{2}-E_{1}=-\frac{A}{4}-(-A)=A-\frac{A}{4}=\frac{3A}{4}$$ (A1)

Since $\dfrac{3A}{4}>\dfrac{3A}{16}$, the $n=2\to1$ line delivers the more energetic photons and must give the larger stopping voltage, $36.3\ \mathrm{V}$; the $n=4\to2$ line corresponds to $5.7\ \mathrm{V}$. (A1)

(c) Applying $eV_{s}=E_{\text{photon}}-\phi$ to each line, and working in electronvolts so that the stopping voltage in volts is numerically equal to the kinetic energy in electronvolts:

$$e(5.7)=\frac{3A}{16}-\phi \qquad\text{and}\qquad e(36.3)=\frac{3A}{4}-\phi$$ (M1)

Subtracting the first equation from the second eliminates $\phi$:

$$e(36.3-5.7)=\frac{3A}{4}-\frac{3A}{16}=\frac{12A-3A}{16}=\frac{9A}{16}$$ (M1)(A1)

$$A=\frac{16\times 30.6}{9}=54.4\ \mathrm{eV}$$ (A1)

Substituting this back into the first equation gives the work function:

$$\phi=\frac{3A}{16}-e(5.7)=\frac{3(54.4)}{16}-5.7=10.2-5.7=4.5\ \mathrm{eV}$$ (A1)

Each stopping voltage is the difference between a photon energy and the work function. A single reading is therefore one equation in two unknowns, $A$ and $\phi$, and cannot be solved; only the difference of the two readings removes $\phi$ and fixes $A$, after which $\phi$ follows from either line. (A1)

(d) For a hydrogen-like ion the energy-level constant is

$$A=13.6Z^{2}\ \mathrm{eV}$$ (M1)

so

$$Z^{2}=\frac{A}{13.6}=\frac{54.4}{13.6}=4.0\quad\Rightarrow\quad Z=2$$ (A1)

The ion is therefore $\mathrm{He}^{+}$, and its ionisation energy is the energy needed to remove the electron from $n=1$ to $E=0$, namely $A=54.4\ \mathrm{eV}$. (A1) Because $A\propto Z^{2}$, a larger $Z$ increases every transition energy. Since $E=hc/\lambda$, each wavelength would be shorter, so both lines would shift to shorter wavelengths, giving more energetic photons and larger stopping voltages. (A1)
questions.explanation:
The difficulty here is not the photoelectric equation, which most candidates can quote, but the fact that a single stopping voltage is an aggregate. It is the photon energy minus the work function, and both are unknown, so one reading gives one equation in two unknowns and is unsolvable. Candidates who have practised only single-line problems will look for a way to pin the work function directly and will not find one; the question is designed so that the only route is to take a difference.

The difference works because the work function appears in both equations with the same sign and the same magnitude. Subtracting removes it exactly, leaving the difference of the two photon energies, which is a pure property of the ion. This is the same trick used in the Millikan experiment to extract the Planck constant from the slope of a stopping-voltage against frequency graph: the intercept carries the work function and the slope carries $h/e$, so a single point cannot separate them. Here the two transitions play the role of two frequencies.

The ion is deliberately left unnamed. The student must recognise that the level spacing of a hydrogen-like ion scales as $Z^{2}$, so recovering $A$ is equivalent to recovering $Z$, and $A=54.4\ \mathrm{eV}$ identifies $\mathrm{He}^{+}$. The two chosen lines, $n=4\to2$ and $n=2\to1$, were picked so that their photon-energy difference is exactly $9A/16$, which makes the arithmetic clean; the ratio of their photon energies, $4:1$, is also a useful check.

Classic wrong turns: assuming that the stopping voltage equals the photon energy, which ignores the work function entirely; trying to find the two wavelengths from the same two equations, which is circular because the wavelengths are what the transition energies already determine; and treating the ion as hydrogen, so that $A=13.6\ \mathrm{eV}$, which is inconsistent with the measured stopping voltages. The last error is easy to make, because the $n=2\to1$ line of hydrogen would give a stopping voltage near $9.1\ \mathrm{V}$, far from the $36.3\ \mathrm{V}$ measured, and a quick numerical check catches it.

questions.subject: Physics HL
questions.topic: Theme E: Nuclear and quantum physics
questions.question:
A nuclear power reactor produces a steady thermal power $P = 3.0\ \mathrm{GW}$ from the neutron-induced fission of uranium-235. A representative fission reaction is
$$^{235}\mathrm{U} + ^{1}_{0}\mathrm{n} \rightarrow\ ^{141}\mathrm{Ba} + ^{92}\mathrm{Kr} + 3\,^{1}_{0}\mathrm{n}.$$
The core is loaded with $1.0\times10^{5}\ \mathrm{kg}$ of uranium enriched to $3.0\%$ uranium-235 by mass, the remainder being uranium-238. The chain reaction is held steady by control rods, and the fast neutrons released are slowed by a moderator before they can induce further fission.

Data (2025 data booklet): atomic mass of $^{235}\mathrm{U} = 235.0439\ \mathrm{u}$; atomic mass of $^{141}\mathrm{Ba} = 140.9144\ \mathrm{u}$; atomic mass of $^{92}\mathrm{Kr} = 91.9262\ \mathrm{u}$; mass of a neutron $= 1.008665\ \mathrm{u}$; $1\ \mathrm{u} = 1.661\times10^{-27}\ \mathrm{kg}$; $1\ \mathrm{u} = 931.5\ \mathrm{MeV}\,c^{-2}$; $1\ \mathrm{MeV} = 1.602\times10^{-13}\ \mathrm{J}$.

(a)

Show that the energy released in this reaction is about $2.8\times10^{-11}\ \mathrm{J}$, and state the same energy in $\mathrm{MeV}$.

[4]

(b)

The reactor operates at a constant thermal power. Determine the number of fission reactions per second and the mass of uranium-235 that undergoes fission each second.

[4]

(c)

Calculate the mass of uranium-235 consumed in one day and the mass converted to energy in one day, and explain why these two masses differ by a factor of about $10^{3}$.

[4]

(d)

Determine the total energy that the uranium-235 in the core can release and the operating lifetime of the core at $3.0\ \mathrm{GW}$. Hence explain what would change, and what would not, if the fuel were enriched to $4.5\%$ instead.

[4]
questions.answer:
(a) The energy released is the mass defect of the reaction multiplied by $c^{2}$; the incident neutron is balanced by one of the three emitted neutrons, so
$$\Delta m = m_{\mathrm{U}} - m_{\mathrm{Ba}} - m_{\mathrm{Kr}} - 2m_{\mathrm{n}}$$ (M1)
$$= 235.0439 - 140.9144 - 91.9262 - 2(1.008665) = 0.18597\ \mathrm{u}$$ (A1)
$$E = \Delta m\,c^{2} = 0.18597 \times 931.5 = 173.2\ \mathrm{MeV}$$ (A1)
$$E = 173.2 \times 1.602\times10^{-13} = 2.78\times10^{-11}\ \mathrm{J}$$ (A1)(AG)

(b) The thermal power equals the energy per fission multiplied by the fission rate, $P = R\,E$, so
$$R = \frac{P}{E} = \frac{3.0\times10^{9}}{2.775\times10^{-11}} = 1.08\times10^{20}\ \mathrm{s^{-1}}$$ (M1)(A1)
Each fission removes one uranium-235 atom of mass
$$m_{1} = 235.0439 \times 1.661\times10^{-27} = 3.904\times10^{-25}\ \mathrm{kg}$$ (M1)
so the mass consumed each second is
$$R\,m_{1} = (1.081\times10^{20})(3.904\times10^{-25}) = 4.22\times10^{-5}\ \mathrm{kg\,s^{-1}}$$ (A1)

(c) In one day the fuel consumed is
$$4.22\times10^{-5} \times 86400 = 3.65\ \mathrm{kg}$$ (A1)
while the mass converted to energy follows from $E = mc^{2}$:
$$m = \frac{P\,t}{c^{2}} = \frac{(3.0\times10^{9})(86400)}{(2.998\times10^{8})^{2}} = 2.88\times10^{-3}\ \mathrm{kg}$$ (M1)(A1)
The ratio is $3.65/(2.88\times10^{-3}) = 1.3\times10^{3}$, close to $235/0.186$: almost all of the fuel mass is carried by nucleons that survive the reaction, and only the mass defect becomes energy. (A1)

(d) The core holds $0.030 \times 1.0\times10^{5} = 3.0\times10^{3}\ \mathrm{kg}$ of uranium-235, or $N = 3.0\times10^{3}/(3.904\times10^{-25}) = 7.7\times10^{27}$ nuclei, so
$$E_{\mathrm{tot}} = N\,E = (7.7\times10^{27})(2.775\times10^{-11}) = 2.1\times10^{17}\ \mathrm{J}$$ (M1)(A1)
At $3.0\ \mathrm{GW}$ the operating lifetime is
$$t = \frac{2.1\times10^{17}}{3.0\times10^{9}} = 7.1\times10^{7}\ \mathrm{s} \approx 820\ \mathrm{days}$$ (A1)
Raising the enrichment to $4.5\%$ leaves the energy per fission unchanged, since it is fixed by the mass defect, and leaves the fission rate needed for $3.0\ \mathrm{GW}$ unchanged; it multiplies the number of fissionable nuclei by $1.5$, so the total energy and the lifetime rise by that factor. (A1)
questions.explanation:
The question turns on a distinction the word energy conceals. A reactor's power is an energy per second, and it factorises into the energy released per fission and the number of fissions per second. The first factor is a property of the nucleus, fixed by the mass defect of the reaction; for uranium fuel it is close to $2.8\times10^{-11}\ \mathrm{J}$, and no amount of enrichment or moderation changes it. The second factor is a property of the reactor, set by how many neutrons survive to cause further fission, which is exactly what the moderator, the control rods and the enrichment influence.

A candidate who has learned that enrichment improves the fuel reaches for it to explain the power, and finds that it does nothing to the energy per fission. The correct account is that enrichment changes the number of fissionable nuclei, and therefore the total energy the core can deliver and the length of time over which it can deliver it, while the power is held steady by the control rods. A moderator acts in the same place in the argument: it slows neutrons so that the fission cross-section is larger, changing how readily the chain reaction proceeds, but the energy released in a single fission is untouched.

The mass bookkeeping is the second trap. The mass of uranium consumed is about a thousand times the mass converted to energy, because the mass defect is only about $0.08\%$ of the fuel mass. A candidate who uses the fuel mass rather than the mass defect in $E = mc^{2}$ overestimates the energy by three orders of magnitude. The ratio $235/0.186 \approx 1.3\times10^{3}$ is a useful check on this.

Classic wrong turns: treating the moderator as adding energy; assuming that doubling the enrichment doubles the power at a fixed control-rod setting; and using the fuel mass rather than the mass defect in $E = mc^{2}$.

questions.subject: Physics HL
questions.topic: Theme E: Nuclear and quantum physics
questions.question:
A red giant star has exhausted the hydrogen in its core and is now fusing helium into carbon through the triple-alpha process,
$$3\,^{4}_{2}\mathrm{He} \rightarrow\ ^{12}_{6}\mathrm{C} + \gamma.$$
During this phase the star's luminosity is $L = 3.0\times10^{28}\ \mathrm{W}$, and its core contains $1.0\times10^{30}\ \mathrm{kg}$ of helium when the burning begins. The star is in hydrostatic equilibrium: the inward gravitational force on the core is balanced by the outward pressure of the radiation produced by the fusion reactions.

Data (2025 data booklet): binding energy per nucleon of $^{4}\mathrm{He} = 7.074\ \mathrm{MeV}$; binding energy per nucleon of $^{12}\mathrm{C} = 7.680\ \mathrm{MeV}$; mass of a $^{4}\mathrm{He}$ nucleus $= 4.0026\ \mathrm{u}$; $1\ \mathrm{u} = 1.661\times10^{-27}\ \mathrm{kg}$; $1\ \mathrm{MeV} = 1.602\times10^{-13}\ \mathrm{J}$; $1\ \mathrm{year} = 3.16\times10^{7}\ \mathrm{s}$.

(a)

Show that the energy released in one triple-alpha reaction is about $7.3\ \mathrm{MeV}$, and explain why the binding energies per nucleon cannot be subtracted directly.

[4]

(b)

Determine the number of triple-alpha reactions per second and the mass of helium consumed per second in this star.

[4]

(c)

Determine how long the helium in the core can sustain the star's luminosity, in years, and state one reason why the real helium-burning phase is shorter than this estimate.

[4]

(d)

Explain how the balance between the outward radiation pressure and the inward gravitational force keeps the core temperature and the fusion rate stable, and hence explain why the star's luminosity does not run away.

[4]
questions.answer:
(a) The energy released is the increase in the total binding energy of the nuclei: (M1)
$$Q = B(^{12}\mathrm{C}) - 3B(^{4}\mathrm{He})$$
Each binding energy per nucleon must be multiplied by its mass number before subtracting: (M1)
$$B(^{4}\mathrm{He}) = 4(7.074) = 28.296\ \mathrm{MeV}, \qquad B(^{12}\mathrm{C}) = 12(7.680) = 92.16\ \mathrm{MeV}$$ (A1)
$$Q = 92.16 - 3(28.296) = 92.16 - 84.888 = 7.27\ \mathrm{MeV}$$ (A1)
That is $7.27/12 = 0.61\ \mathrm{MeV}$ per nucleon, about a tenth of the $6.7\ \mathrm{MeV}$ per nucleon released when hydrogen fuses to helium, so helium must be fused far faster to supply the same luminosity.

(b) The luminosity is the energy released each second, so the reaction rate is
$$R = \frac{L}{Q} = \frac{3.0\times10^{28}}{7.272 \times 1.602\times10^{-13}} = \frac{3.0\times10^{28}}{1.165\times10^{-12}} = 2.58\times10^{40}\ \mathrm{s^{-1}}$$ (M1)(A1)
Three helium nuclei are consumed per reaction, each of mass $4.0026\ \mathrm{u} = 6.648\times10^{-27}\ \mathrm{kg}$: (M1)
$$\dot{m} = 3Rm_{\mathrm{He}} = 3(2.575\times10^{40})(6.648\times10^{-27}) = 5.14\times10^{14}\ \mathrm{kg\,s^{-1}}$$ (A1)

(c) With $1.0\times10^{30}\ \mathrm{kg}$ of helium available,
$$t = \frac{1.0\times10^{30}}{5.14\times10^{14}} = 1.9\times10^{15}\ \mathrm{s} = \frac{1.9\times10^{15}}{3.16\times10^{7}} = 6.2\times10^{7}\ \mathrm{years}$$ (M1)(A1)
The estimate assumes that the whole core mass fuses and that the luminosity stays constant. (A1) Both assumptions make it an overestimate: only the helium in the convective core burns, and the luminosity rises as the core contracts, so the real phase is shorter. (A1)

(d) In equilibrium the energy generated in the core each second equals the energy radiated, so the core neither heats nor cools on average. (A1) If the fusion rate rises, the core temperature rises; the radiation pressure depends strongly on temperature and rises faster than the weight of the overlying layers, so the core expands. (A1) Expansion does work against gravity and lowers the temperature, which reduces the fusion rate back towards its previous value. (A1) The feedback is therefore negative, so the star settles where energy generation matches the rate at which energy can escape, and the luminosity stays stable instead of running away. (A1)
questions.explanation:
The triple-alpha reaction is a good example of a fusion step whose energy yield cannot be read from the masses, because the masses are not supplied: the data give binding energy per nucleon, and each of those must be converted into a total binding energy before subtracting. That conversion is where the question bites. The two per-nucleon values differ by only $0.606\ \mathrm{MeV}$, and a candidate who subtracts them and stops has produced an energy twelve times too small.

The result is small in a second sense too. Hydrogen burning releases about $6.7\ \mathrm{MeV}$ for every nucleon fused, while the triple-alpha step releases only $0.61\ \mathrm{MeV}$ per nucleon, roughly a tenth as much. A star that has moved on to helium burning must therefore consume helium about eleven times faster than it consumed hydrogen to maintain the same luminosity. This is why the later burning stages of a massive star are so much briefer than the hydrogen-burning stage, even though the core holds less fuel.

Part (d) turns to the equilibrium that keeps the star steady. The fusion rate is extremely sensitive to temperature, so a naive account predicts runaway: a slightly higher temperature gives a much higher rate, which gives a still higher temperature. What prevents this is that the same temperature that raises the rate also raises the radiation pressure, which pushes the core outwards. The expansion cools the core and restores the balance. The two effects therefore partially cancel, and the star sits at the temperature at which the energy generated matches the energy escaping.

Classic wrong turns: reporting the per-nucleon difference as the energy released; forgetting that three helium nuclei are consumed in each reaction; and assuming that a higher fusion rate automatically means a brighter star.

questions.subject: Physics HL
questions.topic: Theme E: Nuclear and quantum physics
questions.question:
A sample contains a mixture of two radioactive isotopes, P and Q. Isotope P has a half-life of $4.0\ \mathrm{h}$ and isotope Q has a half-life of $32\ \mathrm{h}$.

At time $t=0$ the total activity of the sample is $1200\ \mathrm{kBq}$. At $t=16\ \mathrm{h}$ the total activity is $300\ \mathrm{kBq}$.

Assume that the decay products are stable and that the two isotopes decay independently.

(a)

Write down an expression for the activity of each isotope at time $t$, in terms of its initial activity.

[2]

(b)

Determine the initial activity of each isotope, showing the pair of simultaneous equations you solve. Give both values in $\mathrm{kBq}$.

[6]

(c)

Calculate the activity of each isotope at $t=16\ \mathrm{h}$ and hence verify that the total is $300\ \mathrm{kBq}$.

[3]

(d)

Determine the time at which the two isotopes contribute equally to the total activity.

[4]
questions.answer:
(a) Using $A=A_{0}2^{-t/T_{1/2}}$:

$$A_{P}(t)=A_{P0}\,2^{-t/4.0},\qquad A_{Q}(t)=A_{Q0}\,2^{-t/32}$$ (A1)(A1)

(with $t$ in hours)

Equivalently $A(t)=A_{0}e^{-\lambda t}$ with $\lambda=\ln2/T_{1/2}$; the two forms are identical because $2^{-t/T_{1/2}}=e^{-(\ln2)t/T_{1/2}}$. For P, $\lambda_{P}=\ln2/4.0=0.173\ \mathrm{h^{-1}}$; for Q, $\lambda_{Q}=\ln2/32=0.0217\ \mathrm{h^{-1}}$. (R1)

(b) Let $A_{P0}=a$ and $A_{Q0}=b$.

At $t=0$: $a+b=1200$ (A1)

At $t=16\ \mathrm{h}$: P has undergone $\dfrac{16}{4}=4$ half-lives and Q has undergone $\dfrac{16}{32}=0.5$ half-lives:

$$a\,2^{-4}+b\,2^{-0.5}=300$$ (M1)(A1)

$$\frac{a}{16}+0.7071\,b=300$$

Substituting $b=1200-a$:

$$0.0625a+0.7071(1200-a)=300$$ (M1)

$$0.0625a+848.5-0.7071a=300 \Rightarrow -0.6446a=-548.5$$

$$a=851\ \mathrm{kBq},\qquad b=1200-851=349\ \mathrm{kBq}$$ (A1)(A1)

Because the decay factors are known numbers, these two equations are linear in $a$ and $b$, which is why two total-activity readings suffice to recover both initial activities. If the two half-lives were equal the equations would be linearly dependent and no unique solution would exist; the eightfold separation of the half-lives is what makes the recovery possible. (R1)

(c) At $t=16\ \mathrm{h}$:

$$A_{P}=851\times2^{-4}=\frac{851}{16}=53.2\ \mathrm{kBq}$$ (A1)

$$A_{Q}=349\times2^{-0.5}=\frac{349}{1.414}=246.8\ \mathrm{kBq}$$ (A1)

$$\text{Total}=53.2+246.8=300\ \mathrm{kBq}\ \checkmark$$ (A1)

(d) Set the two contributions equal:

$$a\,2^{-t/4}=b\,2^{-t/32}$$ (M1)

$$\frac{a}{b}=2^{\,t/4-t/32}=2^{\,7t/32}$$ (A1)

$$\frac{851}{349}=2.438=2^{\,7t/32}$$

$$\frac{7t}{32}=\log_{2}(2.438)=\frac{\ln 2.438}{\ln 2}=\frac{0.8913}{0.6931}=1.286$$ (M1)

$$t=\frac{32}{7}(1.286)=5.88\ \mathrm{h}\approx5.9\ \mathrm{h}$$ (A1)

Check: $A_{P}=851\times2^{-5.88/4}=851\times0.361=307\ \mathrm{kBq}$ and $A_{Q}=349\times2^{-5.88/32}=349\times0.880=307\ \mathrm{kBq}$ ✓

As a limiting check, the crossover must fall after both isotopes are still appreciable and before the fast isotope dominates: $t=5.9\ \mathrm{h}$ lies between $T_{1/2,P}=4.0\ \mathrm{h}$ and $T_{1/2,Q}=32\ \mathrm{h}$, as required. Physically this is the time at which the sample stops behaving like P and starts behaving like Q. (R1)
questions.explanation:
Single-isotope decay questions are routine; this one is not, because there are two unknowns and only one decay curve's worth of data — the *total* activity at two times. That forces a simultaneous solution, and the exponential terms cannot be combined, so there is no shortcut.

The two places where work collapses:

1. Part (b) is really a pair of simultaneous equations. Recognising that 16 h is 4 half-lives for P but only half a half-life for Q is straightforward; the difficulty is then carrying $2^{-0.5}=0.7071$ through the algebra without rounding it to 0.7 (which shifts the answer by about 20 kBq).
2. Part (d) needs the exponent law applied to a difference. $\dfrac{2^{-t/4}}{2^{-t/32}}=2^{-t/4+t/32}=2^{-7t/32}$ — most candidates either add the exponents or subtract them the wrong way round and obtain a negative time, which they then either report or 'fix' by changing a sign without understanding why.

Worth noticing afterwards: the fast isotope P starts with the larger activity (851 vs 349 kBq) but by 16 h it contributes almost nothing (53 kBq against 247 kBq). That is what the crossover time of 5.9 h means physically — the mixture's behaviour is dominated by P early on and by Q later, and any measurement of 'the' half-life of the sample would give a value that drifts continuously from near 4 h towards 32 h. That is why mixed sources are awkward in practice, and why a single half-life measurement on an unknown sample is not enough to identify it.

Classic wrong turns: treating the sample as having a single effective half-life; using $A=A_{0}e^{-\lambda t}$ with $\lambda$ in hours but $t$ in seconds; and rounding $2^{-0.5}$ prematurely.

questions.subject: Physics HL
questions.topic: Theme A: Space, time and motion
questions.question:
A small ball of mass $m=0.050\ \mathrm{kg}$ rests lightly on top of a large ball of mass $M=1.0\ \mathrm{kg}$. The two balls are released from rest together and both fall through a height $h=0.20\ \mathrm{m}$ before the large ball reaches a hard horizontal floor; the balls are small compared with $h$, so they stay on the same vertical line throughout. The large ball strikes the floor and rebounds; that collision is perfectly elastic, so the large ball leaves the floor moving upwards with the same speed it had just before impact. At that instant the small ball has not yet reached the floor and is still moving downwards. The two balls then collide along the vertical line, and that collision is also perfectly elastic. Air resistance is negligible.

(a)

Show that, just before the two balls collide, the large ball is moving upwards at speed $v$ and the small ball is moving downwards at the same speed $v$, where $v=\sqrt{2gh}$, and calculate the value of $v$.

[3]

(b)

By conserving momentum and using the fact that, for a perfectly elastic collision, the relative speed of approach equals the relative speed of separation, show that the velocity of the small ball immediately after the collision is $w=\dfrac{(3M-m)v}{M+m}$ upwards, and calculate the value of $w$.

[5]

(c)

Determine the maximum height above the floor reached by the small ball, express it as a multiple of $h$, and explain why it is greater than $h$.

[4]

(d)

Explain why the multiple of $h$ found in part (c) tends to $9$ as $M/m\to\infty$, and state the largest multiple of $h$ that any mass ratio can give.

[3]
questions.answer:
(a) The large ball falls freely through a height $h$, so just before it reaches the floor its speed is $v=\sqrt{2gh}$. (M1)

The floor collision is perfectly elastic, so the large ball leaves the floor with speed $v$ directed upwards. The small ball has fallen through the same height and is still in free fall, so it is moving downwards at the same speed $v$. (A1)

$$v=\sqrt{2\times 9.81\times 0.20}=\sqrt{3.924}=1.98\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$$ (A1)

(b) Take upwards as positive. Immediately before the collision between the balls the large ball has velocity $+v$ and the small ball has velocity $-v$; let their velocities immediately afterwards be $V$ and $w$. (M1)

Conservation of momentum:

$$Mv+m(-v)=MV+mw\quad\Rightarrow\quad MV+mw=(M-m)v$$ (M1)

For a perfectly elastic collision the relative speed of separation equals the relative speed of approach:

$$w-V=v-(-v)=2v\quad\Rightarrow\quad V=w-2v$$ (M1)

Substituting this into the momentum equation:

$$M(w-2v)+mw=(M-m)v\quad\Rightarrow\quad (M+m)w=(3M-m)v$$

$$w=\frac{(3M-m)v}{M+m}$$ (AG)

Numerically,

$$w=\frac{3.0-0.050}{1.050}(1.981)=\frac{2.95}{1.050}(1.981)=2.810(1.981)=5.57\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$$ (A1)

directed upwards. (The large ball recoils upwards at $V=\dfrac{M-3m}{M+m}v=\dfrac{0.85}{1.05}(1.981)=1.60\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$.)

(c) The small ball leaves the collision with speed $w$ upwards, so it rises to

$$H=\frac{w^{2}}{2g}=\frac{(5.565)^{2}}{2\times 9.81}=\frac{30.97}{19.62}=1.58\ \mathrm{m}$$ (M1)(A1)

As a multiple of the drop height, $H/h=1.58/0.20=7.89$. (A1)

This is far greater than $h$ because the small ball gains energy from the large ball. In the large ball's frame the small ball approaches with relative speed $2v$, and the elastic collision reverses that relative velocity, so the small ball leaves at close to $v+2v=3v$ when $M\gg m$. Its kinetic energy is therefore much larger than the $\frac12 mv^{2}$ it had on landing, and the extra energy is drawn from the much larger kinetic energy of the large ball. (A1)

(d) Dividing numerator and denominator by $M$,

$$\frac{3M-m}{M+m}=\frac{3-m/M}{1+m/M}\to 3\quad\text{as }M/m\to\infty,$$ (M1)

so $w\to 3v$ and $H\to \dfrac{(3v)^{2}}{2g}=9\dfrac{v^{2}}{2g}=9h$. (A1) The largest multiple of $h$ that any mass ratio can give is therefore $9$. (A1) For a finite ratio the multiple is smaller: here $M/m=20$ gives only $7.89$, and a real stacked-ball drop gives far less still because neither collision is perfectly elastic and air resistance removes energy.
questions.explanation:
The result is genuinely surprising: a ball dropped from $0.20\ \mathrm{m}$ rises to $1.58\ \mathrm{m}$, nearly eight times its drop height, with no energy input. Students who have met a bouncing-ball problem usually expect the small ball to return to roughly $h$, or at most to $4h$ if they mis-apply a factor of two. The point is that there are two collisions, not one, and the second one is elastic.

The key insight is to work in the large ball's frame. After the floor bounce the large ball moves upwards at $v$ while the small ball is still moving downwards at $v$, so the relative approach speed is $2v$. In a perfectly elastic collision the relative speed of separation equals the relative speed of approach, so the small ball leaves with relative speed $2v$. Because the large ball is heavy its own velocity barely changes, so in the ground frame the small ball leaves at about $v+2v=3v$. Squaring gives nine times the kinetic energy, hence $9h$.

The exact calculation replaces 'about' with the mass-ratio factor $(3M-m)/(M+m)$. With $M/m=20$ this factor is $2.81$ rather than $3$, so the height is $7.89h$ rather than $9h$; the ideal figure is only approached as the large ball becomes infinitely heavy. A candidate who quotes $9h$ without doing the mass-ratio arithmetic has answered the limiting question, not the one asked, and the markscheme separates the exact value from the limit deliberately.

The classic wrong turns are: assuming the small ball has already landed when the large ball bounces; applying momentum conservation but not the relative-velocity condition, which leaves one equation for two unknowns; and treating the second collision as perfectly inelastic. There is also a real-world check worth making: an actual stacked-ball drop gives far less than $7.9h$ because the coefficient of restitution is well below one and air resistance matters, so the idealised model is an upper bound rather than a prediction.

questions.subject: Physics HL
questions.subtopic: D.2 Electric and magnetic fields / D.3 Motion in electromagnetic fields
questions.question:
The beam enters the selector from the left, travelling along the axis, and the ions are positively charged. The second region is long enough for every ion to complete its semicircular path. Answer all parts using $e=1.60\times10^{-19}\ \mathrm{C}$ and $1\ \mathrm{u}=1.66\times10^{-27}\ \mathrm{kg}$.

(a)

Show that the electric field between the plates has magnitude $E=3.6\times10^{4}\ \mathrm{V\,m^{-1}}$, state the direction of $\mathbf{E}$, and determine the direction of $\mathbf{B}_{1}$ for which a positive ion travelling along the axis passes through the selector undeflected. Explain the relationship between the electric and magnetic forces on such an ion.

[4]

(b)

Show that an ion crosses the selector undeflected only if its speed is $v=\dfrac{E}{B_{1}}$, calculate the value of $v$, and explain why this measurement on its own cannot give the mass of the ion.

[4]

(c)

Each ion that leaves the selector enters the second region and moves along a semicircular path of radius $R$ to the detector. Determine the mass of the ion in kilograms and in atomic mass units, and hence state its approximate mass number.

[4]

(d)

The flux density of the selector's magnetic field is now doubled to $B_{1}'=1.20\ \mathrm{T}$, while $E$ and $B_{2}$ are unchanged. Determine the new radius of the semicircular path and the time the ion spends in the second region, and explain why this time is unchanged even though the radius has altered.

[3]
questions.answer:
(a) The field between parallel plates is uniform, so its magnitude is the potential difference divided by the plate separation:

$$E=\frac{V}{d}=\frac{288}{8.0\times10^{-3}}=3.6\times10^{4}\ \mathrm{V\,m^{-1}}$$ (M1)(A1)

The upper plate is the positive one, so $\mathbf{E}$ is directed vertically downwards, from the upper plate towards the lower plate. (A1)

A positive ion travelling along the axis feels an electric force $q\mathbf{E}$ downwards. For it to cross the selector undeflected the magnetic force $q\mathbf{v}\times\mathbf{B}_{1}$ must be equal in magnitude and opposite in direction, that is upwards. With $\mathbf{v}$ directed to the right and the required force upwards, the right-hand rule gives $\mathbf{B}_{1}$ directed into the page. (A1)

(b) Undeflected motion requires the two forces to balance:

$$qE=qvB_{1}$$ (M1)

Dividing by $qB_{1}$,

$$v=\frac{E}{B_{1}}$$ (AG)(A1)

$$v=\frac{3.6\times10^{4}}{0.60}=6.0\times10^{4}\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$$ (A1)

The balance $qE=qvB_{1}$ contains neither the mass nor the charge of the ion, because both forces are proportional to $q$. The undeflected setting therefore fixes only the speed $v=E/B_{1}$; it carries no information about the mass, and a second measurement that does depend on the mass is needed. (A1)

(c) In the second region the only force is magnetic, and it provides the centripetal force:

$$qvB_{2}=\frac{mv^{2}}{R}\quad\Rightarrow\quad m=\frac{qB_{2}R}{v}$$ (M1)(AG)

$$m=\frac{(1.60\times10^{-19})(0.40)(0.15)}{6.0\times10^{4}}=\frac{9.60\times10^{-21}}{6.0\times10^{4}}=1.60\times10^{-25}\ \mathrm{kg}$$ (A1)

Converting with $1\ \mathrm{u}=1.66\times10^{-27}\ \mathrm{kg}$,

$$m=\frac{1.60\times10^{-25}}{1.66\times10^{-27}}=96.4\ \mathrm{u}$$ (A1)

so the isotope has a mass number of about $96$. (A1)

(d) If $B_{1}$ is doubled to $1.20\ \mathrm{T}$ while $E$ is unchanged, the transmitted speed becomes

$$v'=\frac{E}{B_{1}'}=\frac{3.6\times10^{4}}{1.20}=3.0\times10^{4}\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$$ (M1)

and the new radius is

$$R'=\frac{mv'}{qB_{2}}=\frac{(1.60\times10^{-25})(3.0\times10^{4})}{(1.60\times10^{-19})(0.40)}=0.075\ \mathrm{m}=\frac{R}{2}$$ (A1)

The ion still travels through half a circle, so the time in the second region is half a period:

$$t=\frac{T}{2}=\frac{\pi m}{qB_{2}}=\frac{\pi(1.60\times10^{-25})}{(1.60\times10^{-19})(0.40)}=7.9\times10^{-6}\ \mathrm{s}$$ (A1)

This is the same as before the change. The period of circular motion in a magnetic field is $2\pi m/(qB_{2})$, which contains no speed, so the ion moves round a smaller semicircle at a proportionally smaller speed and arrives at the detector at exactly the same instant. (A1)
questions.explanation:
This question is built around a measurement that cannot see the fields which produce it. The undeflected condition $qE=qvB_{1}$ fixes the speed as $E/B_{1}$, so the selector responds only to the ratio of the two fields. Doubling $E$ and $B_{1}$ together leaves the speed, the straight path and the downstream radius exactly as they were; there is no reading anywhere in the apparatus that would reveal the change. That is the lever: the quantity the student wants to attribute to a single field is in fact set by a ratio.

The second half of the lever is the time spent in the magnetic region. A candidate who has just seen the radius halve when $B_{1}$ doubles naturally expects the ion to reach the detector in half the time. It does not. The period $T=2\pi m/(qB_{2})$ contains no speed, so the ion crawls round a smaller semicircle at a proportionally smaller speed and arrives at the same instant. This is the same reason a cyclotron can accelerate particles to high energy without the orbit period drifting.

The two unknowns in the problem, the speed and the mass, are deliberately split across two measurements. The selector is sensitive only to $v$; the magnet is sensitive to the product $mv$, and therefore, once $v$ is known, to $m$ alone. Neither reading by itself is enough, and the markscheme rewards the recognition that the selector is blind to mass.

Classic wrong turns: treating the selector balance as $qvB=mv^{2}/r$, which confuses the two regions; forgetting that the electric force is also proportional to $q$ and concluding that the selector measures a charge-to-mass ratio; and using the full period rather than half a period for a semicircular path. A useful sanity check is dimensional: $E/B_{1}$ has units of $\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$, and $qB_{2}R/v$ has units of kilograms.

questions.subject: Physics HL
questions.topic: Theme B: The particulate nature of matter
questions.question:
The cycle runs A → B → C → D → A.

(a)

Show that $T_{B}=600\ \mathrm{K}$, $T_{C}=1200\ \mathrm{K}$ and $T_{D}=600\ \mathrm{K}$.

[4]

(b)

Calculate the net work done by the gas in one complete cycle.

[3]

(c)

Calculate the total thermal energy transferred to the gas during one complete cycle.

[5]

(d)

Determine the efficiency of this cycle as a heat engine, and compare it with the efficiency of a Carnot engine operating between the same maximum and minimum temperatures.

[4]
questions.answer:
(a) From $pV=nRT$, with $n$ and $R$ constant, $T\propto pV$.

A → B is isochoric, so $T\propto p$: $\dfrac{T_{B}}{T_{A}}=\dfrac{p_{B}}{p_{A}}=\dfrac{4.0}{2.0}=2 \Rightarrow T_{B}=600\ \mathrm{K}$. (M1)(A1)

B → C is isobaric, so $T\propto V$: $\dfrac{T_{C}}{T_{B}}=\dfrac{V_{C}}{V_{B}}=\dfrac{1.0\times10^{-2}}{5.0\times10^{-3}}=2 \Rightarrow T_{C}=1200\ \mathrm{K}$. (A1)

C → D is isochoric: $\dfrac{T_{D}}{T_{C}}=\dfrac{p_{D}}{p_{C}}=\dfrac{2.0}{4.0}=\dfrac12 \Rightarrow T_{D}=600\ \mathrm{K}$. (A1)

(Consistency check: D → A is isobaric with $\frac{V_A}{V_D}=\frac12$, giving $T_{A}=300\ \mathrm{K}$ as stated.)

(b) Work is done only on the two isochoric-free legs:

B → C: $W=p\,\Delta V=4.0\times10^{5}(1.0\times10^{-2}-5.0\times10^{-3})=4.0\times10^{5}(5.0\times10^{-3})=2000\ \mathrm{J}$ (A1)

D → A: $W=p\,\Delta V=2.0\times10^{5}(5.0\times10^{-3}-1.0\times10^{-2})=-1000\ \mathrm{J}$ (A1)

$$W_{\text{net}}=2000-1000=1000\ \mathrm{J}$$ (A1)

(Equivalently, the area of the rectangle: $(4.0-2.0)\times10^{5}\times(1.0-0.5)\times10^{-2}=1000\ \mathrm{J}$.)

(c) Heat flows in during the two legs where the temperature rises: A → B and B → C.

A → B (isochoric): $W=0$, so by the first law $Q=\Delta U$.

$$Q_{AB}=\tfrac32 nR\,\Delta T=\tfrac32(0.40)(8.31)(600-300)=1.5(0.40)(8.31)(300)=1496\ \mathrm{J}$$ (M1)(A1)

B → C (isobaric): $\Delta U=\tfrac32 nR\,\Delta T=\tfrac32(0.40)(8.31)(1200-600)=2992\ \mathrm{J}$ (A1)

$W=2000\ \mathrm{J}$ from (b), so by the first law $Q=\Delta U+W$:

$$Q_{BC}=2992+2000=4992\ \mathrm{J}$$ (M1)(A1)

$$Q_{\text{in}}=1496+4992=6488\approx6.5\times10^{3}\ \mathrm{J}$$

(d)

$$\eta=\frac{W_{\text{net}}}{Q_{\text{in}}}=\frac{1000}{6488}=0.154=15.4\%$$ (A1)

A Carnot engine between $T_{\max}=1200\ \mathrm{K}$ and $T_{\min}=300\ \mathrm{K}$ has

$$\eta_{\text{Carnot}}=1-\frac{T_{\min}}{T_{\max}}=1-\frac{300}{1200}=0.75=75\%$$ (M1)(A1)

So this cycle achieves only about one fifth of the Carnot efficiency. (A1) The reason is that heat is taken in over a whole *range* of temperatures — including during the isochoric leg A → B, where the gas is still relatively cool — and rejected over a range as well (C → D and D → A). A Carnot engine takes in all of its heat at the single highest temperature and rejects it all at the single lowest; any engine that absorbs heat while its temperature is changing must do worse.
questions.explanation:
This question is assembled from three ideas students usually meet separately, and the joins are where the marks are lost.

First, the temperatures. No absolute calculation is needed if you notice that each leg holds either $p$ or $V$ fixed, so $T\propto pV$ collapses to a simple ratio. Candidates who insist on computing $T=pV/nR$ for every state do more work and accumulate rounding error (the data are only self-consistent to about 0.3%).

Second, and this is the real trap: the net work is not the net heat. Over a complete cycle $\Delta U=0$, so $W_{\text{net}}=Q_{\text{in}}-Q_{\text{out}}$ — but 'the total heat transferred to the gas' means $Q_{\text{in}}$ only, i.e. the two legs on which the temperature rises. A very common answer to (c) is $1000\ \mathrm{J}$, arrived at by applying $\Delta U=0$ to the whole cycle and forgetting the rejected heat entirely. The efficiency then comes out as 100%, which should be an immediate alarm bell.

Third, the Carnot comparison. Students often reach for the temperatures of the *isothermal* legs — but there are none here. The correct bound uses the extreme temperatures the working substance actually reaches, 300 K and 1200 K, giving 75%. The gap between 15% and 75% is then the physical point: a cycle that absorbs heat while warming up is inherently wasteful, which is why real engines use regeneration and why the Carnot ideal insists on isothermal heat exchange.

Classic wrong turns: including C → D in $Q_{\text{in}}$; using $W=p\Delta V$ on the isochoric legs; and quoting the Carnot efficiency with temperatures in the wrong order (giving a negative value).

questions.subject: Physics HL
questions.topic: Theme A: Space, time and motion
questions.question:
A uniform solid disc of mass $M=2.4\ \mathrm{kg}$ and radius $R=0.35\ \mathrm{m}$ is mounted on a fixed horizontal axle. A light string is wound round the rim, does not slip, and hangs vertically with a mass $m=0.80\ \mathrm{kg}$ attached to its free end. The disc is released from rest and the mass falls a distance $h=0.90\ \mathrm{m}$ before it reaches the floor.

(a)

Show that the acceleration of the falling mass is $a=\dfrac{mg}{m+M/2}$ and calculate its value.

[5]

(b)

Calculate the tension in the string while the mass is falling, and explain why it is less than the weight of the mass.

[3]

(c)

Determine the speed of the mass as it reaches the floor, and verify your answer by comparing the loss of gravitational potential energy with the total kinetic energy gained.

[4]

(d)

After the mass lands the string goes slack. A brake then applies a constant torque of $0.24\ \mathrm{N\,m}$ about the axle. Calculate the number of complete revolutions the disc makes before it stops.

[4]
questions.answer:
(a) Let $T$ be the string tension and $a$ the acceleration of the mass; the string does not slip, so the angular acceleration of the disc is $\alpha=a/R$. (M1)

For the hanging mass: $mg-T=ma$ (M1)

For the disc, torque $\tau=TR$ and moment of inertia $I=\dfrac{1}{2}MR^{2}$, so $TR=\dfrac{1}{2}MR^{2}\cdot\dfrac{a}{R}=\dfrac{1}{2}MRa$, giving $T=\dfrac{1}{2}Ma$. (M1)(A1)

Substituting: $mg-\dfrac{1}{2}Ma=ma$, so $a=\dfrac{mg}{m+\dfrac{M}{2}}$. (AG)

Numerically $a=\dfrac{0.80\times 9.81}{0.80+1.2}=\dfrac{7.848}{2.0}=3.92\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$. (A1)

(b) $T=\dfrac{1}{2}Ma=\dfrac{1}{2}\times 2.4\times 3.924=4.71\ \mathrm{N}$. (M1)(A1)

The weight of the mass is $mg=0.80\times 9.81=7.85\ \mathrm{N}$, so $T<mg$. (A1) The tension is less than the weight because the mass is accelerating downwards: the resultant downward force $mg-T$ is what supplies its acceleration, and if $T$ equalled $mg$ the mass would not accelerate at all. Equivalently, the tension is the torque that must be provided to give the disc its angular acceleration, and that comes at the cost of part of the weight.

(c) $v^{2}=2ah=2\times 3.924\times 0.90=7.063$, so $v=2.66\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$. (M1)(A1)

Energy check: loss of potential energy $=mgh=0.80\times 9.81\times 0.90=7.06\ \mathrm{J}$. (M1)

The angular speed of the disc is $\omega=\dfrac{v}{R}=\dfrac{2.6577}{0.35}=7.59\ \mathrm{rad\,s^{-1}}$ and $I=\dfrac{1}{2}(2.4)(0.35)^{2}=0.1470\ \mathrm{kg\,m^{2}}$, so the rotational kinetic energy is $\dfrac{1}{2}I\omega^{2}=\dfrac{1}{2}(0.1470)(57.66)=4.24\ \mathrm{J}$.

Adding the translational kinetic energy of the mass, $\dfrac{1}{2}(0.80)(2.6577)^{2}=2.83\ \mathrm{J}$, gives $7.06\ \mathrm{J}$, which equals the loss of potential energy. (A1)

(d) At the moment the string goes slack the disc has $\omega=7.59\ \mathrm{rad\,s^{-1}}$ and rotational kinetic energy $E_{k}=4.24\ \mathrm{J}$. (M1)

With a constant braking torque, the work done equals the change in rotational kinetic energy: $\tau\theta=E_{k}$, so $\theta=\dfrac{4.238}{0.24}=17.7\ \mathrm{rad}$. (M1)(A1)

$17.7\ \mathrm{rad}=\dfrac{17.66}{2\pi}=2.81$ revolutions, so the disc makes $2$ complete revolutions before stopping. (A1)
questions.explanation:
The question is built around one misconception that survives right up to the final examination: that the falling mass accelerates at $g$. It cannot, because the string tension exerts a torque on a disc that has a finite moment of inertia, and that torque can only be produced if the tension differs from the weight. The disc therefore holds the mass back, and the acceleration depends on the ratio of the two masses. Part (b) makes the point explicit and demands the physical reason rather than the algebra.

The energy check in part (c) is not decoration. A student who computes $v=2.66\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$ from kinematics and then, in the energy check, assumes all the potential energy became translational kinetic energy will find $\sqrt{2gh}=4.20\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$ and a total of $7.06\ \mathrm{J}$ from only $2.83\ \mathrm{J}$ of translational energy. The missing $4.24\ \mathrm{J}$ is the rotational kinetic energy of the flywheel, and locating it is the point of the question: for a solid disc with the string unwinding from the rim, roughly 60% of the energy ends up in the disc.

Part (d) changes regime deliberately. Once the string is slack there is no driving torque and no translational motion, so the problem becomes a rotational work calculation with a constant torque. The two common errors are to keep using the translational kinetic energy, or to use the angular speed in the wrong units. The answer is framed as complete revolutions to force the radians-to-revolutions conversion, which is where the mark is usually lost. A recurring error in part (a) is the wrong moment of inertia: a candidate who reaches for the hoop value $I=MR^2$ instead of the disc value $I=\frac12 MR^2$ obtains $a=\dfrac{mg}{m+M}=2.45\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$, which is still less than $g$ and so does not look obviously wrong.
